ja: אלת'אניה, קום טלבוא תצחיח קראיתהם וצ'בט אלחרכאת, פג'עלוא אכת'ר ג'הדהם פי עלם מואצ'ע אלתנקיט, והם אצחאב אלתנקיט ואלמסורת. ואלמנזלה אלת'אלת'ה קום ראוא נקצאן מן תקדם ד'כרהם, פאג'תהדוא פי תעליל אלתנקיט ואללחון, ואצ'אפוא אליהמא עלם תצריף אללגה ואנחאהא, ועלם אלאסמא ואלאפעאל, וחרוף אלמעאני, ואלאתצאל ואלאנפצאל, ווצף אלמאצ'י בלפט' אלמסתקבל, ואלאמר בלפט' אלמצדר, ואלסאלם ואלמעתל ואלליין ואלמת'לין ואלט'אהר ואלכ'פי, ומא אשבה ד'לך. ואלמנזלה אלראבעה, קום זאדוא עלי מן תקדם ד'כרהם בתפסיר אלחרוף אלמשכלה פי כתאב אללה, ואלט'אהר מן אלנצוץ, ובחת'וא מע ד'לך ען עלם אלמג'אז ואלחקיקי פי אללגה אלעבראניה מן אלאסמא אלמתשאבהה ואלמתכ'אלפה ואלמשתקה ואלמתואטיה ואלשואד, וכד'לך פי אלצפאת ואלאפעאל, ומא אשבה ד'לך. ואלמנזלה אלכ'אמסה, קום זאדוא עלי מן תקדם ד'כרהם בעלם מעאני כתאב אללה ותחציל אצולה, ואלבחת' ען אלמג'אז ואלמחכם פי מעאניה, מת'ל אלתג'סים אלמד'כור פיה, והם אלמפסרון לכתאב אללה מן ט'אהרה דון אלנקל. ואלמנזלה אלסאדסה, קום תעלקוא באלנקל אלקדים אעני אלמשנה, פחצל להם בעץ' ואג'באת אלשראיע ואלפראיץ' ואלאחכאם דון אלנט'ר פי אלתלמוד. ואלמנזלה אלסאבעה, קום זאדוא עלי ג'מיע מא ד'כרנא באלנט'ר פי אלתלמוד, ואג'תהדוא פי חפט'ה וקראהֵ סואדה, דון חל מעאקדה

When we investigate the matter of being moderate in taking from this-world to sustenance, we find it commanded — as the Book says at the beginning of creation: "And God blessed them, and God said to them: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it" (Genesis 1:28); and then He said: "Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed which is upon the face of all the earth — to you it shall be for food" (Genesis 1:29). Moderation in sustenance enters into the gate of the command.

Since this is so, it is valid that the activities of people do not go outside the boundary of the command and the prohibition. The explication of this is: whoever performs an act, if it is among the commands, his act is a good one; if he abandons the act though he was able to fulfill its obligation, he is one who has fallen short. Likewise, whoever performs something among the prohibitions is a sinner; but if he abandons doing it, he is good — when he abandons it out of fear of God, as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "Also they do no iniquity; they walk in His ways" (Psalms 119:3). If he performs something among the permitted and his intent was balanced, he is good, as the Friend said: "Good is the man who is gracious and lends; he shall manage his affairs by justice" (Psalms 112:5). But if he is excessive, going beyond moderation, he is one who has fallen short — for that leads to what God has prohibited. And if he is falling short of moderation, with the capacity to maintain it, but his intent was the disciplining of his soul to the obedience of God, or the suppressing of his appetites in coming near to God, or renunciation of the world and inclination toward the next world, he is good and his act is beautiful. If it is for other than God, he has fallen short and his act is ugly. So the activities of people have been divided into the beautiful and the ugly.

The intelligent one weighs his activities, before performing them, by the like of this weighing, and considers them by the goodness of his thought and the strength of his discernment, so that he chooses the beautiful of them and leaves the rest, like the saying of the Friend (peace be upon him): "I considered my ways, and turned my feet to Your testimonies. I made haste and did not delay to observe Your commandments" (Psalms 119:59–60). The evidence for the soundness of what we have set out of the beauty and ugliness of activities is the Wise One's saying (peace be upon him): "For God shall bring every work into judgment over every hidden thing, whether it be good or whether evil" (Ecclesiastes 12:14). He has confined activities all under "good and evil" — which is what we have mentioned of the concept of the beautiful and the ugly. So it has been made plain that the activities of the people divide into the two divisions of the Law — namely command and prohibition only.

Since the Law is words and meanings, people in the knowledge of the Book differ in ten levels.
